cases.event: One year, the fictional iron railings along the harbor at {E} rusted much faster than the railings in a town farther inland.
cases.q: What most likely caused the railings at {E} to rust so quickly?
restate: The railings at {E} rusted unusually fast, and the question asks why.
Something made the iron railings at {E} rust faster than inland railings.
cases.answer: Salty sea spray most likely caused the railings at {E} to rust so quickly, because salt water speeds up the rusting reaction.
cases.sum: the evidence points to the salty sea spray as the reason the railings rusted so quickly.
cases.myth: The railings at {E} rusted quickly because seagulls painted them red.
cases.mythClause: the railings rusted only on sunny days
cases.altText: Some residents suggested that the railings at {E} had been made from a cheaper kind of iron.
cases.patternQ: What pattern connects the sea spray and the rust on the railings at {E}?
cases.patternA: The railings rusted fastest where the spray reached them and much more slowly once workers rinsed the salt away, so the rust followed the salt.
cases.patternSum: the railings rusted faster where the salt reached them and more slowly where it was rinsed away.

prediction.text: Before the year began, an engineer predicted that every railing in {E} would rust at the same rate.
prediction.claim: every railing in {E} would rust at the same rate
prediction.whyNot: railings sheltered from the spray rusted much more slowly

cases.observerNote: The workers photographed the railings every month.

obs.text: Railings at {E} that stood within {n0} meters of the water rusted the fastest.
obs.tag: the railings closest to the water
exps: the railings closest to the sea get the most spray, and they rusted the fastest
rust was worst exactly where the spray lands, which points to the salt
being close to the water made the difference, which fits sea spray as the cause

obs.text: Tests of the rust on the railings at {E} found large amounts of salt mixed into it.
exps: salt in the rust shows that salt water was part of the reaction that made it
this shows how the spray did its damage, since salt speeds up rusting
finding salt inside the rust ties the damage directly to the sea spray

obs.text: Railings that workers rinsed with fresh water every week rusted far more slowly after about {n1} months.
exps: rinsing away the salt slowed the rust, which is what would happen if salt were the cause
removing the salt reduced the damage, so the two are linked
once the cause was washed away, the effect faded

obs.text: Records showed that the railings at {E} and the inland railings came from the same factory and the same batch of iron.
exps: if both sets of railings used the same iron, the iron cannot explain why only one set rusted fast
this rules out cheap iron, because the iron was identical
with the same iron in both places, the iron explanation has nothing to stand on

obs.text: Railings on the sheltered side of a building at {E}, away from the spray, rusted slowly like the inland ones.
exps: railings made of the same iron rusted slowly when the spray could not reach them
this rules out cheap iron, since the same railings behaved differently depending on the spray
the only thing the sheltered railings lacked was the salty spray
predExps: this directly contradicts the prediction, since the sheltered railings rusted much more slowly
if every railing rusted at the same rate, the sheltered ones would look just as rusty, but they did not
the prediction expected no difference, and a clear difference appeared
